MassScope — feature showcase video script

Source: VIDEO_SCRIPT.md

A shot-by-shot script for a screen-recorded walkthrough (~10 min). The through-line is compound identification from raw LC–MS, and the spine of it is one loop: chromatogram → spectrum → are these peaks one compound? → EICs to check co-elution → back to the spectrum to annotate. At each step the voice-over says which question you’re answering, so the tools land as a workflow rather than a tour. Each shot has [SCREEN] (bulleted actions to perform) and [VO] (voice-over beats — read as connected narration, not a list). Times are approximate.

Recording tips: 1440×900 window, browser zoom ~110 % so the sidebar text is legible, hide the OS cursor trail, and pause ~1 s after each click so the UI settles on camera. Launch with MassScope::run_app() (installed) or, from a clone, Rscript -e "pkgload::load_all('.'); run_app()". Do one dry run first: TIC/EIC extractions are cached on disk, so the second pass (the one you record) is fast.

Test files on this machine

Paste these paths straight into the Files box. The two public datasets come from R packages (installed in the R 4.6 library); the small-molecule runs are in Downloads.

File Path (paste into Files) What it is Use it for
faahKO KO (6 CDF) C:/Users/tmh331/AppData/Local/R/win-library/4.6/faahKO/cdf/KO Centroid MS1, 6 FAAH-knockout samples TIC/BPC overlay, EIC by group, MS map (fast)
faahKO WT (6 CDF) C:/Users/tmh331/AppData/Local/R/win-library/4.6/faahKO/cdf/WT Centroid MS1, 6 wild-type samples Second group for the KO-vs-WT EIC at m/z 335.1
MS3TMT11.mzML C:/Users/tmh331/AppData/Local/R/win-library/4.6/msdata/proteomics/MS3TMT11.mzML Profile MS1 + centroid MS2/MS3, DDA (peptides) Profile line, peak picking, isotope envelope (scan 22413, anchor 582.3448), Precursors map, precursor m/z in hovers
18052015-005.mzML C:/Users/tmh331/Downloads/18052015-005.mzML Urine, positive QTOF, centroid MS1 only, 7 min Adduct / fragment / findMAIN annotation — scan 1408 (rt 5.434 min), base peak [M+H]⁺
20130222-020.mzML C:/Users/tmh331/Downloads/20130222-020.mzML Urine, positive, centroid MS1 + 31 MS2 (all precursor m/z 525), 6 min Small-molecule Precursors view; second urine file for spectrum Facet / Stacked comparison
DIME SCFA…Blank + IS.mzML C:/Users/tmh331/Downloads/DIME SCFA240_20220529_SSCFA_061_neg_Reaction Blank + IS.mzML Truncated mzML (cut off before its closing tags) — unreadable Showing that a broken file gets an error badge and the rest still load

Getting the public paths on another machine: system.file("cdf", "KO", package = "faahKO"), .../"WT", and list.files(system.file("proteomics", package = "msdata"), "mzML$", full.names = TRUE).

Iron-formate (metal complex) demo: neither urine file has a convincing iron-formate series — m/z 131.95 / 132.96 only reach ~10–24 counts (best: 18052015-005.mzML scan acq 150, rt 0.58 min; 20130222-020.mzML scan acq 291, rt 0.68 min). Use a run with real steel-tubing background if you have one; otherwise demo the mechanics on those scans and keep it short.

0. Cold open (0:00–0:20)

[SCREEN] - Title card (MassScope hex sticker), then cut to the app open on TIC / BPC with faahKO loaded and the overlay on screen.

[VO] - MassScope is a local app for reading raw LC–MS data by eye — before any peak picking or alignment. - I use it mostly to figure out what a compound actually is. - There’s one loop I run over and over: chromatogram → spectrum → extract the ions → back to the spectrum. Let me show you that loop.

1. Loading files — three ways, and which one copies (0:20–1:45)

[SCREEN] Empty app, Files panel. Show each control in turn: - Paste the faahKO KO folder path into the box → Add; then the WT path → Add. - Click Choose folder… (native OS folder dialog) — cancel it. - Click Browse files…, and separately drag a file onto it.

[VO] - Three ways to get files in — and the difference matters once your files are large. - Paste a path, or Choose folder…, loads the data in place — nothing is copied; a multi-gigabyte file just stays on disk and the app reads it there. - The path box also takes a single file, and a folder load grabs every MS file in that folder only — it doesn’t descend into sub-folders, so KO and WT go in as two folders. - Browse files… — or dragging files onto it — is the ordinary OS file dialog, and it copies everything into a temp folder first. - So: handy for a file or two, but for big or many files, paste the path and skip the copy.

[SCREEN] - Let the files read in the background — status badges flip to ✅. - Point at the MS, Pol, and Mode (prof/cent/mix) columns. - Double-click a Group cell and rename the WT files’ group to WT (KO → KO). - Click All to include everything; show None and Invert too, then All again.

[VO] - Reading happens in the background — several files at once — so the interface never blocks. - Each row tells me the MS levels, the polarity, and whether the file is profile or centroided, which decides how the views behave. - I set my sample groups right here in the table, and select rows to include files in the plots — All, None, Invert for quick changes. - Two files can even share a name from different folders — they’re kept apart by their parent folder.

[SCREEN] (Optional, 10 s) - Paste the truncated DIME SCFA file path → Add. It gets an error badge and a “Skipped unreadable file” note while the others stay usable.

[VO] - And a broken file doesn’t take the session down — it’s flagged, skipped, and everything else keeps working.

2. Chromatogram → click a peak → spectrum (1:45–3:15)

[SCREEN] - On TIC / BPC, toggle BPC (max) vs TIC (sum). - Set Color by = Sample group; tick Show data points. - Hover a trace — tooltip shows file, scan, rt and intensity. - Click a peak on the trace. - Switch to Spectrum — it’s already loaded at that scan.

[VO] - I start at the chromatogram just to get oriented — where the run is busy, and whether the groups look alike. - Then the core move: I click a peak, and the mass spectrum at that exact scan is waiting on the Spectrum tab. - Everything here is linked like that — a click always takes me to the data underneath.

[SCREEN] Switch to MS3TMT11 (trash button clears the list; paste its path → Add → All): - On TIC / BPC, with MS level all in Filters, hover an MS2 point — the tooltip now also shows its precursor m/z. - On Spectrum, type scan 22413 in …or scan (acquisition) number — the title reads “… • profile” and the scan is drawn as a line. - Tick Show data points (profile). - Open Peak picking → Raw + centroids overlay; zoom one cluster. - Show the S/N, Half-window, and m/z accuracy controls. - Switch to Centroid profile scans for a clean stick spectrum.

[VO] - On DDA data the chromatogram hover even tells me which precursor each MS2 scan fragmented. - I can jump to a spectrum by retention time or by scan number. - Profile data is drawn as a line — thousands of detector samples per peak, which I can even show as points. - To work with masses I centroid it — and because that’s data processing, it lives right here, per view, not in a global filter. - I overlay the centroids first to see exactly what picking keeps, then switch to a clean stick spectrum.

[SCREEN] - Click Table → the peak list (rt, m/z, intensity) for what’s on screen; show Copy and Download CSV; close. - Click Scan list → filter by MS level / precursor m/z / polarity / spectrumId → click a row to jump to that scan; close.

[VO] - The numbers behind the plot are one click away — copy them straight into a spreadsheet, or save a CSV. - And if I don’t have a peak to click my way to, every scan’s metadata is in the scan list — filter it and jump straight there.

3. “Are these peaks the same compound?” → EICs (3:15–4:45)

[SCREEN] Load 18052015-005.mzML (urine). On Spectrum, go to scan 1408: - Set Click on a peak to → EIC list. - Click several peaks — the base peak, a neighbour a couple of Da away, a suspected adduct further out (click, click, click). - Switch to the EIC tab — the targets table is populated and the overlaid EICs render.

[VO] - Here’s the question a single spectrum can’t answer: I see several peaks — but do they belong to one compound (a molecular ion with its adducts, isotopes and fragments), or are they different things that just happen to co-elute? - A spectrum is one slice in time; to tell them apart I need their chromatograms. - So I click each peak into the EIC list and pull them out.

[SCREEN] - Set Scale intensity = Normalise each trace (÷ own max). - Point at the peaks that rise and fall together, versus one that peaks at a different time or with a different shape. - In the targets table, double-click a cell: rename a label, change a tol, type an rt_min / rt_max window to zoom one target.

[VO] - Normalising each trace to its own height throws away abundance and shows me pure shape. - These rise and fall together — same retention time, same profile — that’s one compound. - One that peaks slightly earlier, with a different shape, is a separate species that was just sitting under the same scan. - That co-elution test is the difference between annotating a real adduct series and chasing a coincidence. - Each target is editable — label, tolerance, even its own retention-time window.

[SCREEN] (faahKO, KO + WT included) - Paste 335.1 into the paste box (± tol 10 ppm) → Add to list. - Set Color by = Sample group and Scale = Normalise per target (÷ target max). - Tick Facet by file; then try Log10 (y-axis).

[VO] - The same view answers a different question too — across many samples, is my compound more abundant in one group? - Here’s 335 in the FAAH knockouts versus wild-type, clearly up where the biology says it should be. - I can split it per file, or log-scale it to see the small ones.

4. Back to the spectrum → annotate the ion set (4:45–6:15)

[SCREEN] Return to Spectrum, urine scan 1408: - Tick Annotate adducts / fragments. - Note Ion mode auto-set from the scan polarity; leave Manual anchor (base peak default) — the base peak labels [M+H]⁺. - Point at the labelled adduct / fragment / isotope peaks and the “N candidate peaks feed matching” readout. - Open the matching options: ± tol, Match S/N, Min int (% base), Annotate only top N peaks, isotope tolerance / Max isotope M+n / Max charge, In-source fragments. - Tick Show expected-but-absent.

[VO] - Now that I know which peaks belong together, I annotate them. - I anchor on the molecular-ion candidate; the app projects the common adducts and in-source fragments and labels the ones actually present. - The ion mode follows the scan, and matching runs against real centroids at a signal-to-noise I control — with a readout of how many peaks feed it, so nothing is hidden. - I can also show what should be there but isn’t — an absent sodium adduct is evidence too.

[SCREEN] - Switch Mode → Auto-suggest (findMAIN) → Suggest molecular ion → click a ranked row. - Then switch to Difference network → show the peak-pair Δ labels.

[VO] - If I’m unsure which peak is the molecule, findMAIN ranks the hypotheses for me. - Or I drop the anchor entirely and annotate the differences between peaks — to catch a neutral loss or an adduct relationship I hadn’t assumed.

5. From a mass to a formula — fine isotopes and contaminants (6:15–7:15)

[SCREEN] Back on MS3TMT11, scan 22413, peak picking Raw, Show data points on: - Mode → Isotope pattern (formula); anchor 582.3448, adduct [M+H]⁺. - Show the candidate-formula table (formula, mass, ppm, DBE, ✓). - Pick a row → the translucent green envelope overlays the raw cluster; zoom to ~580.5–586.5. - Adjust Resolving power; click From data to estimate it from the peak width.

[VO] - With the right ion and its neutral mass, I want a formula. - The app decomposes the mass into candidates, then overlays the fine isotope pattern for each — the true ¹³C, ¹⁵N, ³⁴S structure, simulated at my instrument’s resolving power. - The envelope is translucent, so I can see the raw peaks underneath and judge the fit. - That’s how a mass becomes a confident formula.

[SCREEN] (see the iron-formate note under Test files) - Add Fe to the Elements selector. - Choose the [M]+ adduct and turn off Chemically valid only. - Anchor 131.9504 or 132.9582 → an iron-formate formula at low ppm.

[VO] - Half of identification is ruling out contaminants. - Iron-formate clusters leach from steel tubing and carry an intrinsic charge from the metal’s oxidation state. - Add iron, pick the metal-ion type, relax the organic-only rule — and the background ion names itself.

6. MS map — surveying the neighbourhood (7:15–8:00)

[SCREEN] faahKO included: - Go to MS map, press Plot. - Drag the Contrast slider on the 2-D m/z × rt map; show rt bin, m/z bin, Intensity percentile cutoff, Line/point size. - Note Peak picking = Centroid profile scans is on by default. - Switch to 3D surface, press Plot, and rotate it; then 3D points. - Back on 2-D, click a pixel → Spectrum loads that scan.

[VO] - Sometimes I zoom out from one peak and survey the neighbourhood — co-eluting isomers, an adduct series marching across m/z, a contaminant ladder. - The map bins exact centroids over mass and time; I set the bin sizes, lower the contrast for the weak stuff, or rotate a 3-D view. - It only draws when I press Plot, because a full map can be millions of points. - And, as everywhere, click a point to read the spectrum underneath.

7. Precursors — MS2 for structure (8:00–8:40)

[SCREEN] - With MS3TMT11 (DDA) included, go to Precursors. - Show the rt × precursor-m/z scatter; Color by file. - Type a range into Precursor m/z (e.g. 500–700) — the map narrows. - Set a global m/z filter in Filters — the map does not change. - Click a point → its MS2 loads on the Spectrum tab. - (Small-molecule version: include 20130222-020.mzML — its MS2 all sit on precursor m/z 525.)

[VO] - For the structural layer of an ID I need fragmentation. - The Precursors map shows exactly what the instrument fragmented and when. - It has its own precursor-mass range: the global m/z filter selects peaks, which on an MS2 means fragments — a different thing — so it’s kept separate. - Click a precursor and I’m reading its MS2, ready to annotate it the same way.

8. Filters, settings, export (8:40–9:45)

[SCREEN] - Open Filters: set an rt window and MS level, add a Spectrum ID rule (e.g. function=1); watch a plot update; Reset filters. - Open Settings: switch the time unit (minutes ↔︎ seconds) and palette, tick Invert colour scale; show the Parallel readers slider and the EIC/export defaults.

[VO] - Two housekeeping notes. - Global filters — retention time, m/z, intensity, MS level, polarity, even spectrum-ID rules — narrow every view at once. - Settings — time unit, ColorBrewer and viridis palettes, how many files read in parallel, and the defaults for new EICs and exports — persist across restarts.

[SCREEN] - Zoom into a plot, then press Save → the export dialog previews exactly the zoomed view; drag its corner to resize; show png / svg / pdf / rds, width, height, units, DPI.

[VO] - When I’ve made the case, Save exports what I’m looking at — zoom included — as a publication image, or the raw ggplot object to keep tweaking in R.

9. Close (9:45–10:00)

[SCREEN] - Zoom out to the full app; end card with the hex sticker, the repo URL (github.com/stanstrup/MassScope) and the site (stanstrup.github.io/MassScope).

[VO] - That’s the loop — chromatogram, spectrum, extract the ions to prove they belong together, then annotate to a formula and a structure. - Raw LC–MS, one click at a time. - It installs from GitHub or runs from a Docker image, and the website has a guide for every tab.
